It looks like you're searching mainly for reference apps, but for any incoming medical students in here or for those who are looking for apps to aid in revision rather than reference, I'm currently using:

Memrise - this flashcard style app uses spaced repetition to ensure that you review all of your concepts at equal times (look for the anatomy and physiology courses by Durham university, those are quite clean and well moderated)

OSCE for Medical Students - This is more of a revision aid for medical students who are going to take their OSCEs

If you're in the UK you can get the BNF (British National Formulary) app on your phone for free with an NHS athens password. Also medicines.org.uk is great for info about drugs but I think the offline app version costs £5

I recommend you the next apps:

-MedCalc: it is the most complete medical calculator. It will be really useful for your obstetrics rotation when you have to calculate the weeks of gestation for every pregnant patient. It has also every formula for calculating GFR, which is great for internal medicine or nephrology. I can't think of a formula/calculation it doesn't have. The downside is the complete version is like 5 USD.

-NEJM This Week: if you don't have a subscription to NEJM, with this app you can freely access every article on the current NEJM edition. You also have access to the tutorial videos (which are pretty educative and teach you procedures such as spinal taps), images in clinical medicine and audio recordings. This is a must have.

-LabTests: this is an app I bought for 1 USD. It has the reference values of almost every lab test, and has a quick summary explaining the lab tests and the possible diagnosis of an abnormal lab test. It is not the best reference, but it works just fine for a quick review.

-JN Challenge: this is the JAMA Network image challenge. It is an images quiz. They show you 5 medical images and you have to answer questions based on them. The questions are pretty difficult in my opinion. They are mostly rare cases and exceptions, but it is good for practice because it offers an extensive discussion about every case.

I used to regularly stay up to 8AM in the morning, it can turn into a pretty vicious cycle. The trick, besides being forced to change schedule by work or whatnot, is to just make sleep interesting and something that you want to do. Read a good book or watch chill documentaries while in bed, or if you're feeling particularly adventurous, experiment with lucid dreaming methods or something. Pretty much just turn sleep into a thing that tickles your mind, because those are the only things we really actively enjoy doing.

Also, a light sleep supplement like melatonin can help greatly, especially if you spend a lot of time around monitors.
